For necessity, let the first player write five copies of \(24\) and four copies of \(23\). Their total is
\[
5\cdot24+4\cdot23=212.
\]
The full list has sum \(212\), while every proper subset has sum at most \(212-23=189\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\), so \(N=10\) (and therefore every smaller \(N\)) is insufficient.

For sufficiency, take \(N=11\), so the required interval is \([189,211]\). If the total sum of the list is at most \(211\), selecting the entire list works, since its sum is at least \(200\).

Now suppose the total exceeds \(211\). Choose an inclusion-minimal subset whose sum \(T\) exceeds \(211\). If no desired subset existed, then for every element \(a\) of this subset, minimality gives \(T-a\le211\), and avoidance of \([189,211]\) forces
\[
T-a\le188.
\]
Thus \(a\ge T-188\). Since \(a\le25\), we obtain \(T\le213\). As \(T>211\), either \(T=212\) or \(T=213\).

If \(T=212\), every element of the subset is at least \(24\). At most eight such elements sum to at most \(200\), while at least nine sum to at least \(216\), so their sum cannot be \(212\).

If \(T=213\), every element is at least \(25\), hence equals \(25\), but no sum of copies of \(25\) equals \(213\). Both cases are impossible. Therefore some subset always has sum in \([189,211]\), proving that \(N=11\) is sufficient.","reason":""}

{"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(G\) and \(H\) be nonabelian groups of order \(21\). By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow \(7\)-subgroup.

For \(G\), choose generators \(b\) of a Sylow \(7\)-subgroup and \(a\) of a Sylow \(3\)-subgroup. Their intersection is trivial, so \(G=\langle b\rangle\langle a\rangle\), and every element has a unique expression \(b^s a^r\), where \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\).

Since \(\langle b\rangle\) is normal, conjugation by \(a\) gives
\[
aba^{-1}=b^i
\]
for some \(i\in\{1,\dots,6\}\). Because \(a^3=e\), conjugating three times gives \(b=b^{i^3}\), hence \(i^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(i=1,2,4\). \[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

\[
c^3=d^7=e,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2,
\]
and every element of \(H\) has a unique expression \(d^s c^r\).

Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(b^s a^r)=d^s c^r.
\]
This is well-defined by uniqueness of the normal forms. Since
\[

\]

\[
(b^s a^r)(b^t a^u)=b^{s+2^r t}a^{r+u}.
\]
The identical formula holds in \(H\), so \(\phi(xy)=\phi(x)\phi(y)\). Hence \(\phi\) is a homomorphism. It is bijective because it maps the unique \(21\) normal forms \(b^s a^r\) to the unique \(21\) normal forms \(d^s c^r\). Therefore \(G\cong H\).
